summary.objective: Automatically alert the appropriate people ahead of a freelance mission's end date, so action (renewal, extension, replacement, or final invoicing) can be taken before the mission lapses.

briefs.problem: Freelancer missions can reach their end date with no renewal, extension, replacement or offboarding decision made in time, because nothing proactively flags an approaching end.
briefs.solution: A scheduled alert that fires ahead of a mission's end date and routes a notification to the relevant people so an action gets taken before the mission lapses.
introduces: a date-driven trigger/scheduling mechanism that scans Mission end dates
a configurable lead-time rule engine (per client/contract/mission type)
role-based notification routing tied to Contact role, not just Client
idempotency and re-trigger logic to survive mission date changes (extension, early end, cancellation)

challenges.headline: Undefined notification recipients
challenges.premise: The request assumes 'the right people' is self-evident and can be routed generically.
challenges.alternative: Enumerate explicit recipient roles per event — e.g. mission manager always notified, client contact notified only if their role is billing/operational, freelancer notified separately or not at all — and make that list configurable per client rather than assumed.
challenges.consequence: Building generic routing without a defined recipient set risks alerting the wrong people (or missing the client contact who actually acts on renewal), which quietly defeats the feature's entire purpose.
challenges.recommendation: Run a short workshop with the client to enumerate exact recipients per role and confirm whether the list varies by client or mission type before any routing logic is built.

challenges.headline: Single fixed trigger vs. moving dates
challenges.premise: The design implicitly treats the mission end date as stable once the alert is scheduled.
challenges.alternative: Model the trigger as reactive to end-date mutation — recompute or cancel/reschedule the alert whenever the date changes — rather than a one-time scheduled job fired at creation.
challenges.consequence: Mission dates are volatile by nature (extension, early end, cancellation, renewal); a naive one-shot scheduler will send stale, duplicate, or missing alerts in what is likely the most common real scenario, not an edge case.
challenges.recommendation: Define explicit behaviour for date changes (cancel/reschedule/no-op) and design the trigger as idempotent against repeated date edits before implementation.

challenges.headline: Notification sent vs. lapse prevented
challenges.premise: The request equates 'notify the right people' with solving the stated problem of missions lapsing unnoticed.
challenges.alternative: Treat the alert as the start of a tracked follow-up — log whether a decision (renewal, extension, offboarding) was actually made before the end date, and escalate if it wasn't — rather than a fire-and-forget message.
challenges.consequence: A notification that nobody acts on still lets the mission lapse silently; without any acknowledgment or escalation path, the feature can succeed technically while failing the actual business goal.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify with the client whether success means 'alert delivered' or 'outcome logged before end date' — this changes scope materially.

no current process or success metric to bound scope

opportunities.text: Generalize the 'approaching event date' trigger (lead-time + config + idempotent recompute) as a reusable engine — Contracts have an equally recurring need to flag approaching renewal or end dates.
Standardize role-based notification routing (by Contact role) as a shared service, since routing-by-role is already a recurring need across Mission, Contract and Invoice events.
A configurable lead-time rule model built here could later back other date-driven alerts (contract renewal reminders, amendment deadlines) without rebuilding the concept.

next_steps: Confirm the exact recipient list per role and whether it varies by client or mission type before designing routing.
Define the lead-time rule (fixed vs. configurable per client/contract) with the client's operations team.
Specify behaviour when a mission's end date changes after the alert is scheduled — cancel, reschedule, or leave as-is.
Clarify the success measure: is a delivered notification sufficient, or does the feature need to track whether a decision was actually made in time?

briefs.solution: An automated look-ahead alert that warns the relevant stakeholders before a mission's end date, likely configurable per client or contract.

a per-client/contract configuration surface for lead time and recipient rules

challenges.headline: Undefined notification audience

challenges.alternative: Route on the Contact's existing role (billing/HR/operational) the platform already models, rather than inventing a new recipient concept for this one alert.
challenges.consequence: Building the routing logic before the audience is confirmed risks notifying the wrong contact — a real exposure given some recipients are external Client contacts.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client to name the exact roles/contacts before any routing logic is designed.

challenges.headline: Assumed single global lead-time rule
challenges.premise: Nothing confirms whether the advance-notice window is one fixed number of days or varies by client/contract.
challenges.alternative: Treat lead time as a per-client/contract configurable value from day one, since this platform already varies business rules by client and retrofitting configurability later touches the same screens twice.
challenges.consequence: Scoping this as a hardcoded rule and later discovering it must vary by client turns a small feature into a rebuild of its rule storage and admin UI.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether a single rule suffices or configurability is required before estimating.

challenges.headline: One-shot trigger ignores mission changes
challenges.premise: The workflow implicitly treats 'mission is about to end' as a single fire-and-forget event, with no stated behavior for what happens if the mission is later extended, ended early, or renewed.
challenges.alternative: Model the alert as a re-evaluated state (recompute against the current end date) rather than a one-time fire, so extensions or early cancellations naturally supersede a stale alert instead of producing a false one.
challenges.consequence: Without this, an extended mission still fires (or worse, doesn't re-fire) the original alert, undermining trust in the feature the first time a mission changes — which the context flags as common.
challenges.recommendation: Define the mission-change/idempotency rule explicitly before building the trigger, not as an afterthought.
